entries.note: The host is located from its own descriptor and confirmed against ps, never pgrep/pkill: on macOS those exclude the caller's ancestors by default (man pgrep, -a), and every pane inside a workspace is a descendant of its host, so `pkill -f main.mjs` typed there matches nothing and exits 1 silently. Measured 2026-09-07: `pgrep -f server/main.mjs` listed 13 hosts and not PID 68944; `pgrep -a -f` and ps both showed it. A tool built on pgrep would inherit the trap. The --state tail of the command line is compared canonically (realpath, falling back to resolve) so a descriptor that names another directory's host, a reused PID, or a worktree's preflight host is refused with nothing signalled (spec 098 decision 2).

anchor.snippet: for (const supervisor of await findSupervisors(instance, processes, options)) {

entries.note: Order matters: the update supervisor bound to this host instance is stopped first, because its SIGTERM handler closes its desktops and workers and its recovery path would otherwise try to replace a worker against a host that is on its way out. Supervisors are matched by runtime.json host.instance under this checkout's .cache/runtime and confirmed as supervisor.mjs in the process table; another checkout's supervisor is never touched. Children still alive after each stop are swept so a SIGKILL fallback leaves no orphan PTYs (spec 098 decision 4).

anchor.snippet: if (!await portReleased(url, options)) throw new Error(`${url} still accepts connections after PID ${pid} exited; not starting a second host.`);

entries.note: The stale sidecar.json is removed only after the old PID is gone AND its port refuses connections. ensureSidecar treats a descriptor whose PID is alive-but-unavailable as a reason to refuse a second host, so a reused PID could otherwise block the restart; and starting while the port still answers would be two hosts for one directory (spec 098 decision 5).
